overview.title: The MNIST tensor: rank 3, shape (60000, 28, 28), dtype uint8
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.main_topic: Reading the three key attributes off the real MNIST training tensor (`ndim` 3, `shape` (60000, 28, 28), `dtype` uint8), interpreting it as 60,000 grayscale 28 x 28 matrices with values 0-255, and displaying one digit with Matplotlib (Listing 2.8, Figure 2.2) alongside its label.
overview.central_idea: The abstract attributes rank, shape and dtype become concrete on the MNIST data: a rank-3 tensor of 8-bit integers is an array of 60,000 image matrices, and selecting `train_images[4]` yields one 28 x 28 matrix that renders as the digit 9, whose label `train_labels[4]` is 9.
overview.importance: This is the page where the reader connects the tensor vocabulary of p.46-47 with data they have already trained on, and where the idea 'first axis = samples' is used for the first time (`train_images[4]`), setting up slicing and batches on p.49. Visualizing a sample with `imshow` is also a habit the book relies on throughout the vision chapters.
learning_objectives: Inspect a NumPy tensor's `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` and interpret the results.
Explain why (60000, 28, 28) with dtype uint8 means 60,000 grayscale images of 28 x 28 pixels with values 0-255.
Select one sample along the first axis (`train_images[4]`) and display it with `plt.imshow`.
Relate an image sample to its label via the shared index (`train_labels[4]` is 9).
prerequisites: The three key attributes rank, shape and dtype (p.47).

summary:
The page applies the three key attributes of p.47 to the MNIST data. First the dataset is loaded again with `from keras.datasets import mnist` and `(train_images, train_labels), (test_images, test_labels) = mnist.load_data()`.

Then the attributes of `train_images` are read one by one: `train_images.ndim` is `3`; `train_images.shape` is `(60000, 28, 28)`; `train_images.dtype` is `uint8`. The authors interpret this: a **rank-3 tensor of 8-bit integers**, more precisely an array of **60,000 matrices of 28 x 28 integers**, each matrix being a **grayscale image** with coefficients between 0 and 255.

**Listing 2.8** displays the fourth digit of this tensor with Matplotlib (part of the standard scientific Python suite): `digit = train_images[4]`, then `plt.imshow(digit, cmap=plt.cm.binary)` and `plt.show()`. **Figure 2.2** shows the result: a handwritten 9 on a 28 x 28 pixel grid, with pixel coordinates 0-25 marked on the axes.

Naturally, the corresponding label is just the integer 9: `train_labels[4]` returns `9`. The image and label arrays are aligned by index, which is the one-to-one correspondence stated on p.42. The next page (p.49) generalizes `train_images[i]` to tensor slicing and introduces the samples axis and data batches.

paragraphs.excerpt: Next, we display the number of axes of the tensor train_images, the ndim
paragraphs.what_it_says: After reloading MNIST, the authors display the number of axes of `train_images` via the `ndim` attribute: it is 3.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The training images form a rank-3 tensor, exactly the 'array of matrices' structure introduced on p.47. Three indices are needed to reach a pixel: which image, which row, which column.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Rank tells you how to think about the data and which layers can consume it; the Dense model of p.43 needed rank 2, which is why p.44 reshaped this rank-3 tensor.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `ndim == 3`, consistent with the shape tuple having three entries.

terminology.meaning: The number of axes (rank) of the array.

connections: p.47: rank defined as the first key attribute.
p.44: reshape to rank 2 before feeding the Dense model.

paragraphs.what_it_means: Axis 0 has 60,000 entries (one per image), axis 1 has 28 (rows of pixels), axis 2 has 28 (columns of pixels). The tuple has three entries, matching `ndim`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the shape that was reshaped to (60000, 784) on p.44; reading it correctly is what makes `28 * 28` in Listing 2.4 obvious.
paragraphs.technical_idea: 60000 x 28 x 28 = 47,040,000 pixel values in total.

terminology.meaning: Tuple with the size of the tensor along each axis.

connections: p.47: shape defined as the second key attribute.
p.49: the first axis is the samples axis.

paragraphs.excerpt: And this is its data type, the dtype attribute:
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each pixel is an unsigned 8-bit integer, so it ranges over 0-255 and occupies one byte; the whole tensor is about 47 MB. This is the natural storage format of grayscale images and the reason p.44 divided by 255 after casting to float32.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: dtype governs memory and arithmetic; knowing the raw data is uint8 explains both the preprocessing step and why one must cast before dividing.

terminology.meaning: Unsigned 8-bit integer type with values from 0 to 255.

connections: p.47: dtype defined as the third key attribute.
p.44: `astype("float32") / 255` converts this dtype and range.

paragraphs.excerpt: So what we have here is a rank-3 tensor of 8-bit integers. More
paragraphs.what_it_says: Putting the three attributes together: a rank-3 tensor of 8-bit integers; precisely, an array of 60,000 matrices of 28 x 28 integers, each a grayscale image with coefficients between 0 and 255.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This sentence is the template for reading any data tensor: rank says how many levels of structure, shape says how big each level is, dtype says what each cell holds. Here the levels are image -> row -> pixel. 0 is black (or white, depending on the colour map) and 255 the opposite extreme.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It demonstrates the interpretive skill the section is teaching, and the phrase 'array of 60,000 matrices' is exactly the packing construction of p.47. Note (p.51) that by convention image tensors are usually rank 4 with a channels axis; MNIST's grayscale images are stored here without it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `train_images[i]` is a (28, 28) uint8 matrix; `train_images[i, r, c]` is one pixel intensity in 0-255.

terminology.meaning: An image with a single intensity channel per pixel, stored as a matrix.

connections: p.47: rank-3 tensors as packed matrices.
p.51: image data conventions, including the channel axis absent here.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let's display the fourth digit in this rank-3 tensor, using the library Matplotlib
paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors display the fourth digit of the tensor with Matplotlib, part of the standard scientific Python suite; Listing 2.8 and Figure 2.2 follow.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Indexing the first axis with `[4]` pulls out one 28 x 28 matrix (indexing starts at 0, so this is the fifth image in human terms, the 'fourth' in zero-based counting). `imshow` maps each matrix entry to a pixel brightness; with `plt.cm.binary`, 0 is white and 255 black, so the stroke appears dark on a light background, as in Figure 2.2.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Looking at samples is the first thing to do with any dataset; the figure also makes the abstract 28 x 28 matrix tangible, with the pixel axes 0-25 visible around the digit.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `train_images[4]` selects along axis 0 and returns a rank-2 tensor of shape (28, 28); p.49 calls this tensor slicing.

terminology.meaning: The standard Python plotting library; `pyplot` is its state-based interface.
Matplotlib function that renders a 2-D array as an image.

connections: p.49: `train_images[i]` generalized to slicing along any axis.
p.42: Figure 2.1 showed several MNIST sample digits.

paragraphs.excerpt: Naturally, the corresponding label is just the integer 9:
paragraphs.what_it_says: The label corresponding to the fourth image is the integer 9, obtained by `train_labels[4]`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Images and labels are two separate tensors kept aligned by index: `train_images` has shape (60000, 28, 28), `train_labels` has shape (60000,), and position 4 in both refers to the same sample. The label is a scalar integer, not an image or a one-hot vector.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This alignment is what supervised learning rests on; `fit()` on p.44 relied on `train_images[i]` and `train_labels[i]` describing the same digit. It also shows why `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` was the right loss: labels are plain integers.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `train_labels` is a rank-1 uint8 tensor; `train_labels[4]` is a rank-0 value, 9.

terminology.meaning: The class associated with a sample (p.42); for MNIST an integer 0-9.

connections: p.42: 'The images and labels have a one-to-one correspondence.'
p.44: integer labels used directly with `sparse_categorical_crossentropy`.

concepts.name: Reading rank, shape and dtype of a real tensor
concepts.definition: The practice of inspecting `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` to understand what a data tensor contains.
concepts.intuition: Three questions to ask any array: how many levels, how big each, what kind of number.
concepts.technical: For `train_images`: `ndim` 3, `shape` (60000, 28, 28), `dtype` uint8, hence 60,000 grayscale 28 x 28 images with values 0-255.
concepts.significance: This is the diagnostic routine used before any preprocessing or model building; it explains every step of Listing 2.4 (p.44).
concepts.misconception: `shape` and `ndim` are attributes, not methods; `train_images.shape()` raises an error.

concepts.name: Indexing the first axis to get one sample
concepts.definition: Selecting `train_images[i]` returns the i-th sample, a (28, 28) matrix, because the first axis of a data tensor enumerates samples.
concepts.intuition: The tensor is a stack of photos; `[4]` pulls the fifth photo off the stack.
concepts.technical: Indexing drops the first axis: (60000, 28, 28) -> (28, 28). p.49 names axis 0 the samples axis and generalizes to slices such as `train_images[10:100]`.
concepts.significance: The samples-first convention holds for every data tensor in deep learning and underlies batching (p.49).
concepts.example: `digit = train_images[4]` in Listing 2.8; `train_labels[4]` is its label, 9.
concepts.misconception: `train_images[4]` is the fifth image, because indexing starts at 0; the book still calls it 'the fourth digit' in zero-based language.

concepts.name: Grayscale image as a matrix
concepts.definition: A grayscale image is a matrix of pixel intensities; MNIST stores each digit as a 28 x 28 uint8 matrix with values 0-255.
concepts.intuition: A grid of 784 tiny squares, each with a darkness level.
concepts.technical: `imshow` renders the matrix; with `cmap=plt.cm.binary`, 0 maps to white and 255 to black. Image tensors in general are rank 3 (height, width, channels) and batches rank 4 (p.51); MNIST omits the channel axis.
concepts.significance: It is the simplest image representation and the bridge to the rank-4 colour image tensors of the vision chapters.
concepts.example: Figure 2.2: `train_images[4]` rendered as a handwritten 9 on a 28 x 28 grid.
concepts.misconception: The pixel values are not probabilities or normalized intensities until divided by 255 (p.44); here they are raw bytes.

math.title: What the MNIST shape means

variables.meaning: Sample index along axis 0, from 0 to 59,999.
Pixel rows and columns of each image.
The range of a uint8 pixel value.

math.operations: Indexing along the first axis removes it, turning a rank-3 tensor into a rank-2 matrix; indexing the label vector gives a scalar.
math.purpose: Formalize the sentence 'an array of 60,000 matrices of 28 x 28 integers' and the image/label alignment.
math.interpretation: The same index i addresses an image and its label; the model's job is to learn the map from the 28 x 28 matrix to the integer.
math.intuition: Think of the tensor as 60,000 small photographs filed in order, with a list of 60,000 answers filed in the same order.
math.numerical_example: Total pixel values: 60000 x 28 x 28 = 47,040,000; at one byte each (uint8) that is about 47 MB, versus about 188 MB once converted to float32 on p.44 (not in the book).

digit = train_images[4]
plt.imshow(digit, cmap=plt.cm.binary)
plt.show()
code.what_it_does: Selects the image at index 4 (a 28 x 28 uint8 matrix) and renders it with Matplotlib in a black-on-white colour map, producing Figure 2.2 (a handwritten 9).

Index the first (samples) axis; `digit` has shape (28, 28) and dtype uint8.
`imshow` draws the matrix as an image; `cmap=plt.cm.binary` maps low values to white and high values to black so the pen stroke appears dark.
Render the figure window (or inline plot in a notebook).

# AI-written: show the first 10 digits with their labels in one figure

for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    ax.imshow(train_images[i], cmap=plt.cm.binary)

code.what_it_does: Returns the label at index 4 of the label vector: the integer 9, matching the image displayed in Figure 2.2.

line_explanations.explanation: Same index as `train_images[4]`; images and labels are aligned by position.

deeper.title: From attributes to an English sentence
deeper.body:
The page shows how to turn three attribute readouts into the description 'an array of 60,000 matrices of 28 x 28 integers'. The same recipe works for any tensor:

1. **Read `ndim`** (3): there are three levels of nesting, so each sample is itself a rank-2 object.
2. **Read `shape`** ((60000, 28, 28)): the outer level has 60,000 entries; each entry is a 28 x 28 grid.
3. **Read `dtype`** (uint8): each cell is an integer from 0 to 255.
4. **Add domain knowledge**: a 28 x 28 grid of 0-255 integers is a grayscale image; 60,000 of them are the training samples.

Applying the recipe to `train_labels` gives: rank 1, 60,000 entries, uint8 integers, which are the digit classes 0-9. Applying it to the preprocessed data of p.44 gives: rank 2, 60,000 rows of 784 floats in [0, 1].

deeper.title: Why Figure 2.2 shows axes from 0 to 25
deeper.body: Beyond the book: Matplotlib's `imshow` treats the matrix as an image whose pixel centres sit at integer coordinates, so the axes are pixel indices. The tick labels run 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 along both directions because the image is 28 pixels wide (indices 0-27) and Matplotlib picks ticks every 5. Row index increases downward, matching how the matrix is printed and how `train_images[4][r, c]` is addressed: `r` counts rows from the top, `c` columns from the left. Reading the figure this way, the loop of the 9 occupies roughly rows 5-14 and the tail descends to about row 25.

deeper.title: A filing cabinet of photographs
deeper.body: Imagine a filing cabinet with 60,000 numbered slots. Each slot holds a tiny 28 x 28 photograph where each square has a darkness between 0 and 255. That cabinet is `train_images`: its rank is 3 (slot, row, column), its shape is (60000, 28, 28), and its dtype is 'one byte per square'. Next to it is a ledger (`train_labels`) with 60,000 lines, one per slot, each line a single digit. Listing 2.8 opens slot 4 and holds the photo up to the light; the ledger's line 4 says '9'. Training on p.44 was the process of leafing through the cabinet and ledger together, 128 slots at a time.

visualizations.title: From the (60000, 28, 28) tensor to one 28 x 28 digit and its label
visualizations.why: Traces exactly what Listing 2.8 does: indexing the samples axis of the rank-3 tensor to obtain the (28, 28) matrix shown in Figure 2.2, and the parallel label vector giving a scalar.

visualizations.title: A small image tensor: height, width and the (absent) channel axis
visualizations.why: The page describes each MNIST sample as a 28 x 28 grayscale matrix; p.51 notes that image tensors conventionally carry a channels axis (1 for grayscale, 3 for colour). Explore how an (H, W, C) tensor is laid out in channel slices.

misconceptions.claim: `train_images[4]` is the fourth image in ordinary counting.
misconceptions.correction: Indexing starts at 0, so index 4 is the fifth stored image; the book's 'fourth digit' uses zero-based language. What matters is that `train_labels[4]` refers to the same sample.

misconceptions.claim: A uint8 value of 255 always means white.
misconceptions.correction: 255 is simply the maximum intensity; how it is displayed depends on the colour map. With `plt.cm.binary`, 255 renders black and 0 white, which is why the digit in Figure 2.2 is dark on a light background.

misconceptions.claim: Because the images are rank 3, each image is a rank-3 tensor.
misconceptions.correction: The batch tensor is rank 3; each individual image is a rank-2 (28, 28) matrix. The samples axis accounts for the extra rank.

misconceptions.claim: The labels must be converted to images or one-hot vectors before use.
misconceptions.correction: `train_labels` is a vector of integers 0-9 and is used as-is with `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` (p.44). One-hot encoding is an alternative discussed later (p.143).

earlier.note: Listing 2.1 first loaded MNIST; images and labels correspond one to one; Figure 2.1 shows sample digits.
Listing 2.4 reshaped this (60000, 28, 28) uint8 tensor to (60000, 784) float32.
Definitions of rank, shape and dtype applied on this page.

later.note: Tensor slicing (`train_images[10:100]`, cropping pixels) and the notion of the samples axis and batches.
Real-world data tensors: images as rank-4 (samples, height, width, channels).
Image data conventions; grayscale images stored with a channel axis of size 1 by convention.
Section 2.5 restates the input data as float32 tensors of shape (60000, 784).

related_math.note: Shape as a tuple and rank as its length.

related_figures.note: Figure 2.4, a rank-4 image data tensor.

takeaways: `train_images` has `ndim` 3, `shape` (60000, 28, 28) and `dtype` uint8: a rank-3 tensor of 8-bit integers.
Read together, the attributes mean 60,000 grayscale images, each a 28 x 28 matrix of integers between 0 and 255.
`train_images[4]` selects one sample along the first axis, giving a (28, 28) matrix that `plt.imshow(digit, cmap=plt.cm.binary)` renders as the digit 9 (Figure 2.2).
`train_labels[4]` is 9: images and labels are aligned by index.
Inspecting `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` is the first step in understanding any data tensor.

questions.question: What does `train_images.shape == (60000, 28, 28)` with `dtype == uint8` tell you?
options: 60,000 colour images of 28 x 28 pixels with 3 channels
60,000 grayscale images of 28 x 28 pixels with integer values 0-255
questions.answer: 60,000 grayscale images of 28 x 28 pixels with integer values 0-255
questions.explanation: The page interprets the attributes as 'an array of 60,000 matrices of 28 x 28 integers', each a grayscale image with coefficients 0-255. There is no channel axis (no colour), the first axis is the samples axis, and the flattened float32 form only exists after Listing 2.4 on p.44.

questions.question: What is the shape and rank of `digit = train_images[4]`, and why?
questions.answer: Shape (28, 28), rank 2: indexing the first axis of the rank-3 tensor removes that axis, leaving one image matrix.
questions.explanation: The page describes the tensor as an array of 60,000 matrices; selecting one entry along the first axis returns one of those matrices. `imshow` requires a 2-D array, which is why this works.

questions.question: Why does the page cast the image data to float32 on p.44 but leave `train_labels` as integers?
options: Labels are never used during training
The loss `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` consumes integer class labels directly, while the network's arithmetic runs in float32
uint8 labels are automatically converted to images
questions.answer: The loss `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` consumes integer class labels directly, while the network's arithmetic runs in float32
questions.explanation: `train_labels[4]` is simply the integer 9, and p.44 chose a 'sparse' loss precisely so integer labels can be used. The pixel data is cast so that the network's float32 computations and the [0, 1] rescaling work correctly.

questions.question: How many pixel values does `train_images` hold, and roughly how much memory does it take as uint8?
questions.answer: 60000 x 28 x 28 = 47,040,000 values; at 1 byte each, about 47 MB.
questions.explanation: The element count is the product of the shape entries; uint8 uses one byte per value. (Memory figures are not stated on this page; the same reasoning appears on p.52 for a video tensor.)

questions.question: Explain what `cmap=plt.cm.binary` does in Listing 2.8 and why the digit in Figure 2.2 appears dark on a light background.
questions.answer: The colour map decides how intensities 0-255 are turned into colours; `binary` maps 0 to white and 255 to black, so the high-valued pen strokes show up dark.
questions.explanation: `imshow` has no intrinsic notion of 'ink'; the colour map determines the rendering, and the book chooses `binary` to get a natural pen-on-paper look.

questions.question: Why is it guaranteed that `train_labels[4]` describes the image `train_images[4]`?
questions.answer: Because the image and label arrays were loaded together with a one-to-one correspondence by position (p.42); both have 60,000 entries along their first axis indexed identically.
questions.explanation: The page says 'naturally, the corresponding label is just the integer 9', relying on the alignment stated when the data was introduced.

questions.question: Without running code, write down the `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` you expect for `test_images` and `test_labels`, then explain how you would display the first test digit.
questions.answer: `test_images`: ndim 3, shape (10000, 28, 28), uint8; `test_labels`: ndim 1, shape (10000,), uint8. Display with `plt.imshow(test_images[0], cmap=plt.cm.binary); plt.show()`.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment transferring the page's routine to the test arrays (their sizes come from p.44, where 10000 is used in the reshape).
